title: Disney Sues FCC, Alleging Political Retaliation Over ABC's Coverage
summary:
Disney has taken the Federal Communications Commission to court, alleging that the agency's move to accelerate license reviews for eight ABC-owned stations is a politically motivated attack on free speech. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, DC, claims the early review is an effort by the Trump administration to intimidate the company after its news coverage infuriated the president.

The 46-page complaint details a pattern of escalating attacks: "Again and again, the Administration has attacked ABC's speech - the stories its journalists report and the viewpoints its network programs air." It cites Truth Social posts from 2025 in which Trump said the network "should lose their Licences for their unfair coverage of Republicans and/or Conservatives." The FCC, however, says the April license renewal call was based on diversity, equity, and inclusion practices at Disney and an investigation into ABC's talk show "The View."

The lawsuit also points to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr's March threat that stations airing "fake news" could lose their licenses, and Trump's demand that ABC fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over comments he made before the White House correspondents dinner shooting. Free speech advocates have rallied behind Disney. Seth Stern, director of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, told Al Jazeera: "It's about time for someone to take Brendan Carr and his FCC to court over their endless campaign of intimidation and retaliation against journalism that displeases Carr's thin-skinned boss." He called Carr a "censorship tsar" who abuses his office to target Trump's perceived adversaries.

Disney is seeking a speedy hearing and a temporary restraining order. The lawsuit sent Disney's stock up 1.1 percent in morning trading. The case could set a major precedent for press freedom and the limits of regulatory power.
why_it_matters: This case matters because press freedom depends on the government being unable to punish newsrooms for coverage it dislikes. If regulators can use license reviews to intimidate media companies, criticism of leaders—especially in a democracy—becomes risky, and that affects what information citizens receive.

background_read: In the United States, local television stations need licenses from the Federal Communications Commission, an independent government agency that oversees broadcasting and wireless communication.
ABC, one of the country's best-known broadcast networks, is owned by Disney; the eight ABC-owned stations at issue are normally reviewed on a regular schedule.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly attacked ABC and other mainstream outlets, accusing them of unfair coverage and suggesting they should lose licenses.
Brendan Carr, the FCC chairman appointed by Trump, has also warned that stations airing what he calls fake news could face license trouble.
The dispute touches ABC's daytime program The View, known for blunt political commentary, and late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, a comedian with a long history of mocking Trump.
The Freedom of the Press Foundation, a nonprofit that defends journalists and free expression, has backed Disney.
The case may test whether a regulatory agency can use its licensing power to pressure a media company about editorial choices.

perspectives.perspective: Positive / Disney and free speech advocates
perspectives.description: Disney and groups like the Freedom of the Press Foundation argue that the government is using licensing power to punish scrutiny of the president. They see the lawsuit as a necessary defense of editorial independence and the First Amendment.

FCC officials maintain the review is ordinary regulatory oversight tied to diversity, equity, and inclusion practices and programming at The View. Supporters of a tough media stance may believe ABC has long been biased and that license scrutiny is legitimate accountability.

The case exposes how licensing authority, even when not used directly to revoke a license, can create a chilling effect on journalism. By moving reviews forward, a regulator may signal political displeasure without admitting intent.

A federal court ruling could define clearer limits on when regulators may accelerate or target license reviews. Depending on the outcome, other broadcasters may feel safer to criticize any administration—or more cautious about provoking regulators.
